papers.title: Sparse Phosphorylatable Residues, Tuned by Agonist Chemotype, Shapes GPCR Signaling
papers.abstract: GPCR signaling diversity is often attributed to an intracellular phosphorylation barcode, in which ligand-dependent modification of multiple receptor phosphoresidues encodes selective engagement of downstream transducers. However, whether such an extensive phosphorylation of the receptor is universally required remains unclear. Here, we show that the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), a central regulator of energy homeostasis, achieves remarkably diverse and pathway-selective signaling through a sparse set of strategically positioned regulatory phosphoresidues. Systematic study of these phosphoresidues within helix 8 and the C-terminal tail revealed distinct, spatially segregated contributions to receptor function. Substitution of helix 8 residues S306 disrupted beta arrestin2 recruitment, early endosomal trafficking, and ERK1/2 activation, while visibly altering G alpha-cAMP signaling in all the receptor variants. In contrast, distal C-terminal substitutions had little effect on beta-arrestin2 coupling and trafficking, revealing that these regions are not functionally redundant. Surprisingly, signaling through G alpha q/11- and G alpha12/13-linked pathways remained largely constrained across receptor variants, further demonstrating pathway-specific control by these phosphoresidues. Notably, ligand chemotype reshaped the functional consequences of these substitutions: setmelanotide selectively restored or enhanced signaling through pathways that were compromised by specific receptor mutations. Together, our findings argue that GPCR signaling diversity does not necessarily require an extensive phosphorylation barcode. Instead, MC4R uses a minimal number of spatially organized phosphoresidue that can differentially control transducer engagement and downstream signaling, while ligand chemistry determines how this regulatory landscape is accessed.

papers.title: How social value guides curiosity, information search, and memory in younger and older adults
papers.abstract: Epistemic curiosity, or the desire for new knowledge, benefits emotional, physical, and cognitive health across the lifespan. Initially believed to be solely intrinsically motivated, recent work has found that extrinsic motivators can also drive epistemic curiosity. One example of the latter is the perceived social value of information, such as popularity metrics on social media platforms (e.g., upvotes on Reddit.com). However, it remains unclear whether the influence of social value cues extends to curiosity-related behaviors, such as information search and memory, and whether these effects vary with age. The current study was designed to fill these knowledge gaps. In two experiments, younger and older adults (total N = 367) rated their curiosity for user-generated trivia questions that varied in social value (high or low upvote counts on Reddit.com). Upvote counts were either visible (upvote visible condition) or not visible (upvote invisible condition). In Experiment 1, participants had the opportunity to reveal the answer to each trivia question, a measure of information seeking. Although social value increased curiosity, it did not influence information seeking. In Experiment 2, answer reveal was mandatory, and participants received a surprise recall test for the answers. Social value again increased curiosity, particularly for younger adults, but had no influence on memory. Overall, these findings replicate social-value effects on curiosity in younger and older adults, but they provide no evidence that social value motivates information search or episodic memory. These findings highlight the limits of extrinsic influences on epistemic behaviors across the adult lifespan.

papers.title: The Impact of Small-group Education on Student Wellbeing in Undergraduate Biology: a Student Perspective on Self-Determination Theory
papers.abstract: Alarming reports about mental health have raised awareness of student wellbeing in STEM Education. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) implies that wellbeing can be improved by fulfilling the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness. Educational design elements such as small-group teaching, peer feedback and offering a low-stakes practice environment can help fulfill these SDT needs. These elements were applied in a new academic skills course in our undergraduate Biology program. Here, we investigated how this affected the students sense of autonomy, competence and relatedness, and whether this was related to wellbeing. First, a survey among 48 students confirmed that student wellbeing is positively correlated to SDT fulfillment. Next, group interviews with students revealed that wellbeing is mostly dependent on relatedness, which is facilitated through small-group teaching in the first semester. Furthermore, students reported that (1) relatedness evolves through bonding with peers over the shared experience of struggle, (2) competence requires (peer) feedback and opportunities for growth, especially in laboratory coursework and (3) a structured, low-stakes environment supports competence, but without optimal challenge, also undermines a sense of autonomy. This illustrates how students perceive the effects of small-group educational activities on their wellbeing through the lens of Self-Determination Theory.

papers.title: Evidence for a cohesion-related function of alpaca hums: Linking automated call detection with GPS data
papers.abstract: Understanding how animals communicate while moving helps explain social dynamics, but simultaneously tracking vocal and spatial behaviour in freely moving groups remains challenging. Animal-borne audio and GPS recordings can place naturally occurring vocalisations in their spatial context, but continuous recordings generate large datasets that require automated call detection.We used this approach to investigate whether alpaca hums, a poorly characterised vocalisation, contribute to group cohesion. We combined automated detection of hums from continuous collar-borne audio with synchronised GPS data from a partially collared herd to test whether humming is associated with changes in spacing and movement consistent with a contact-call function. We combined deep-learning-assisted detection with manual validation to build a large curated hum corpus from 2,011 h of continuous recordings from a partially collared herd. We then tested how humming was associated with spacing and movement at both individual and group levels. Following hum production, distance between focal alpaca and the group shifted toward closer contact relative to matched non-hum periods. Hums were also more likely to occur when the collared alpaca moved faster. These findings support a cohesion-related role of hums and suggest that this call type may help alpaca maintain social contact while moving. More broadly, our study shows how automated call detection combined with movement data can place poorly characterised vocalisations in a behavioural context, narrow their plausible functions, and generate targeted hypotheses even when caller identity remains uncertain and only part of a group can be collared. This approach extends functional research on vocal communication to species whose calls remain poorly understood.

papers.title: Risk management strategies in social grooming among Tonkean and rhesus macaques
papers.abstract: Group-living individuals interact constantly, maintaining cohesion, stability, and security within their social groups. However, these interactions can entail risks that individuals must manage to optimize their social navigation through complex social groups, such as those of non-human primates. Here, we investigated how macaques manage risk during social grooming by analysing its somatic modalities, including body orientation and body site being groomed. We compared two macaque species with contrasting social styles: the more despotic rhesus macaque and the more tolerant Tonkean macaque. Using dyadic analyses including species, kinship, age difference, rank difference, and male presence as predictors, we found marked species differences in grooming patterns. Tonkean macaques engaged more frequently in face-to-face grooming and less in face-to-back grooming compared to rhesus macaques. They also groomed body sites associated with high eye-contact probability, such as the head, neck, and chest, more often than rhesus macaques. Kin dyads groomed these body sites more often, particularly in rhesus macaques. These findings suggest that avoiding body sites associated with potential eye-contact may constitute a risk management strategy during grooming. Overall, our results reveal a previously overlooked dimension of primate social cognition that may shape dyadic relationships and social network structure.

papers.title: The effect of dominance rank on behavioural response to playback calls in ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta)
papers.abstract: In group-living species, dominance hierarchies play a central role in shaping social dynamics, influencing both agonistic and affiliative interactions. Being able to recognise an individual's dominance rank at a distance, can reduce direct conflicts, facilitating group coordination, and mediating social cohesion. While the role of dominance in relation to aggressive or reproductive vocalizations has been well documented, its influence on affiliative contact calls, particularly in mediating group movement and social integration, remains underexplored. We conducted playback experiments with free-ranging adult ringtailed lemurs (Lemur catta) at the Affenwald Wildlife Park to investigate how dominance rank of the caller and rank differences between caller and listener affect behavioral responses. Using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs), we analysed three response variables: vocal response, number of visual scans, and occurrence of movement. Our results revealed sex-specific effects: females exhibited increased movement following contact calls from high-ranking individuals, and tended to refrain from moving when their own rank exceeded that of the caller. In contrast, no significant effects of dominance rank were observed in males. These findings suggest that high-ranking females may play an important role in initiating group movement. This study provides insights into the role of dominance rank in mediating social coordination through contact calls and provides a foundation for further research into the role of vocal communication in maintaining group cohesion in primates.

papers.title: Percussive manipulations distinguish object play in capuchin and patas monkeys
papers.abstract: Object play has been proposed as a developmental precursor of flexible tool use. We applied a standardized object play protocol, previously used with corvids and parrots, to tufted capuchin monkeys (Sapajus apella), a member of a genus known for tool use, and patas monkeys (Erythrocebus patas), for which tool use has not been reported. Both groups were tested in a zoo across 15 sessions with a standardized set of objects and activity plates. All capuchins smashed objects, whereas only two patas monkeys did so, a difference consistent with the per-cussive foraging of capuchins. The species did not differ significantly in behavioral variability, object combinations, manipulation time, number of body parts used, or tail use, and combination rates were low in both. The species thus differed in a specific form of manipulation rather than in overall or combinatory object play. With one species per category and small samples, these results cannot establish whether combinatory object play is associated with tool use in primates.

papers.title: LNP Delivery of Prime Editors Enables Durable Correction of PAH R408W in Phenylketonuria Models
papers.abstract: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a monogenic metabolic disorder caused by mutations in the phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) gene, the most common of which is c.1222C>T (p.R408W). Current treatment options, including dietary restriction and enzyme substitution, can be effective but are often challenging for patients to maintain and do not address the underlying genetic defect. Gene editing represents a compelling one-time treatment approach for PKU. Herein, we demonstrate mRNA:LNP-mediated delivery of prime editors that enable therapeutically-relevant levels of correction of the R408W mutation in both in vitro and in vivo model systems. Further, we found that co-delivery of the DNA repair modulator RAD18 and engineering of the prime editor protein, enabled 2-fold and 3-fold increases in prime editing relative to PE3 respectively, resulting in ~50% correction efficiency in a humanized PKU mouse model. Collectively, this work identifies novel potential approaches to enhancing prime editing and establishes LNP-delivered prime editing as a mutation-specific, non-viral therapeutic strategy for PKU, as well as providing a framework for extending prime editing to other inherited liver diseases.

papers.title: Cell Painting PLUS reveals phenotypic signatures for nephrotoxicity profiling in human RPTEC/TERT1
papers.abstract: Multiplex high-throughput phenotypic profiling offers a cost-effective approach to monitor how chemical perturbations alter cellular morphology, thereby contributing to a mechanistic, human-centred hazard assessment with new approach methodologies in the context of Next Generation Risk Assessment (NGRA). In this study, we employed Cell Painting PLUS (CPP), an expanded high-content imaging assay that adds spatially resolved channels for mitochondria, lysosomes, actin, Golgi, RNA, DNA, and the endoplasmic reticulum, to renal RPTEC/TERT1 cells to evaluate nephrotoxicity. We profiled a set of nephrotoxic agents together with well-annotated reference chemicals encompassing diverse cellular targets to identify specific morphological profiles associated with distinct mechanisms of action (MoAs). Benchmark concentration modelling, correlation analysis, and hierarchical clustering of RPTEC/TERT1 CPP data captured specific morphological signatures of more than 300 tested compounds and enabled discrimination between closely related and opposing phenotypes. Comparison with CPP data generated in bone osteosarcoma U2OS cells highlighted cell-type-specific differences: despite lower overall activity, RPTEC/TERT1 resolved biologically relevant nephrotoxicity-associated phenotypes, highlighting the importance of using physiologically relevant cell models for contextspecific phenotypic profiling. Overall, these findings establish RPTEC-based CPP as a valuable phenotypic profiling platform supporting mechanistic nephrotoxicity assessment for integration into NGRA.

papers.title: Funding deadlines act as a zeitgeber for science
papers.abstract: Funders decide which science is paid for. Whether they also shape when it becomes public has been hard to test. Across 376,542 preprints on bioRxiv and medRxiv, the US share rose by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points in the four weeks before due dates for the main research grant of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and dropped on the date. About one in eleven US preprints in those weeks was attributable to the deadline, and fields that depend least on NIH rose least. Among 15,906 funded investigators, the share of preprints posted in the four weeks before their own deadline was 9% higher than in other four-month cycles, and these preprints resembled the later grant without being more highly cited. Repeated before every due date, this individual surge matches the national peak's timing within a week. NIH's application calendar, like its funding, shapes when US biomedical science becomes public.

papers.title: Distinct amygdala-striatal and amygdala-cortical circuits encode and retrieve predictive learning to guide choice and decision-making
papers.abstract: It has long been known that Pavlovian cues can influence choice between instrumental actions, although how this is achieved at a neural level is not fully understood. Here we examined the neural processes engaged during the encoding and retrieval of the Pavlovian stimulus-outcome (S-O) associations prior to and during their influence on choice. Using a Pavlovian-instrumental transfer paradigm (PIT), we found, as previously reported, that a circuit connecting the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and nucleus accumbens shell (BLA[->]NAc-S) is necessary to encode specific S-O associations within the NAc-S. However, this circuit was not required for the retrieval of those associations: optogenetic inhibition of this circuit had no effect on the ability of specific S-O associations to influence choice between instrumental actions. The BLA also projects to the infralimbic cortex (IL) although, using circuit mapping, we found that this projection was largely independent of the projection to the NAc-S. Nevertheless, using a circuit-specific disconnection approach, we found that the BLA[->]IL circuit is necessary for both the encoding and retrieval of specific S-O associations to influence choice. Furthermore, expanding on this disconnection approach, optogenetic inhibition of the BLA[->]IL circuit in one hemisphere and the IL[->]NAc-S contralaterally provided evidence that the broader BLA[->]IL[->]NAc-S circuit is necessary to retrieve specific S-O associations to influence choice during PIT. These data reveal, therefore, evidence of an amygdala-cortico-striatal circuit necessary for the retrieval of predictive learning to influence choice that differs from the circuit involved in encoding those predictive associations.

papers.title: Social and reproductive benefits of group fission in wild geladas
papers.abstract: Living in large, crowded groups can result in fitness costs due to increased competition and conflict. When dispersing from large groups isn't possible, fissioning into two or more smaller 'daughter' groups may provide an important mechanism for mitigating these costs. Here, we leveraged 15 years of behavioral and demographic data to identify both (i) the social factors that predict group membership decisions and (ii) the adaptive consequences of group fission in the gelada (Theropithecus gelada), a grass-eating primate in which the risk of male infanticide -- the largest fitness cost to females -- is highest in larger groups. After fissioning, females tended to join the same daughter groups as their close kin, closely ranked females, and other strong grooming partners, both female and male. However, females did not join the likely fathers of their dependent infants, even though doing so is expected to prevent infanticide. Group fissions were not preceded by increases in female-female aggression or salient changes in activity budgets but were preceded by increases in infant mortality. In particular, infanticide was elevated prior to fission and plummeted after groups split. Taken together, these data illustrate how animals navigate competing social priorities and highlight the role of fission in ameliorating the costs of group-living.

papers.title: It runs in the family: New extinct species from charismatic clades are more likely to be published in high-impact journals than those from non-charismatic clades
papers.abstract: The cultural landscape of paleontology is dominated by dinosaurs and a few other charismatic clades that are more likely to be depicted in media and to be recognized by the public. There is a prevailing belief among researchers that these biases extend to scholarly publishing - that certain clades enjoy a 'taxonomic advantage' that renders them more likely to be published in high-impact journals like Nature and Science. Given the importance of publishing in high-impact journals for career advancement, quantitative testing of this hypothesis can inform on potential biases in this area. I examined articles describing new species that were published between 2000 and mid-2026 in one of thirteen journals (n = 4,248 articles, 8,331 new species), ranging from high-profile, multidisciplinary titles like Nature to lower-profile, specialist titles like the Journal of Paleontology. Comparisons of the taxonomic composition of new species between journals revealed a positive correlation between a journal's prestige (approximated by its impact factor) and the relative proportion of new species that belong to charismatic clades. Avemetatarsalians and mammaliamorphs represent more than 50% of new species in Nature and Science but less than 15% of new species in the control group of paleontological journals. These results provide support for the perception that there is a bias between extinct taxa as it relates to publication in high-impact journals. Given the potential for researchers to accrue cumulative advantage through publishing in prestigious journals, bias in favor of charismatic clades creates the potential for opportunities and knowledge generation to become increasingly skewed and consolidated towards these clades, at the expense of less charismatic clades and the people studying them. This threatens the discipline's ability to continue to construct a holistic understanding of the full history of life that can be disseminated to the public. Further attention should be directed towards examining potential biases in paleontological publications as the primary currency in academia.

papers.title: NIH's dedicated K23 trial pathway was associated with more K-trial leadership but no detectable gain in new trials
papers.abstract: Research funders often train investigators by funding a project, expecting the experience to produce leaders of the next one. Delivering the funded project and leading new work are different outcomes. In 2018 the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) created a dedicated clinical trial pathway for its K23 mentored career development awards. Using registry records for 1,847 K23 awardees and a language-model measurement corrected against blinded human review, we compared awardees whose awarded plans proposed their own trial with those whose plans did not, before and after the change. The pathway was followed by more leadership of the award-supported trial (difference in differences, 13.7 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, 5.7 to 21.2) but no detectable gain in leadership of distinct new trials (-3.8; -14.4 to 6.9), including over seven years. The K-trial estimate exceeded the new-trial estimate by 17.4 points (5.3 to 29.7) under every measurement correction. The additional supported trials were registered with the awardee as principal investigator and started at rates similar to earlier ones, whereas whether more awardees led any trial depended on the correction. Because groups were defined by awarded plans, the design cannot fully separate changes in behaviour from changes in who was funded. A training pathway can raise delivery of the work it funds without a detectable increase in leadership of further trials. As NIH consolidates its career awards and ends K support for trial conduct, evaluations should measure both outcomes.

papers.title: Expecting the unexpected: Great apes anticipate surprise in others
papers.abstract: Humans adeptly navigate complex social environments by attempting to anticipate the actions and emotional responses of others. Although our closest ape relatives have sophisticated social cognitive abilities, we do not know whether they have a cognitive understanding of others' emotions. For the epistemic emotion surprise, a cognitive understanding would require sensitivity to an agent's belief, to reality, and to any misalignment between the two, allowing one to model the mental conditions that drive surprise. In a non-invasive eye tracking study with 31 chimpanzees and bonobos, apes showed evidence of a cognitive understanding of surprise: they detected the misalignment between an agent's belief and reality, exhibiting greater pupil dilation right before an agent encountered an unexpected outcome relative to an expected one. This suggests that apes and humans share a more complex understanding of others' mental lives than previously thought, capacities that likely evolved millions of years ago in a common ancestor.

papers.title: Pick your battles: competitive strategies of green chromides (Etroplus suratensis) during inter- and intraspecific contests
papers.abstract: Competitive ability is a key determinant of organismal fitness, yet high costs of interference competition necessitate strategic behavioural responses. This study investigated how green chromide (GC), a cichlid native to the Indian subcontinent, competes with the globally invasive tilapia species (T, Oreochromis spp.) that has encroached upon its habitats. We staged dyadic feeding competitions between GC and T, and analysed aggression, feeding, and hiding behaviours of both the species and further contrasted them with intraspecific contests in GC. We varied developmental stages, residency status of opponents, and used different combinations of body sizes of competitors to test their effects on the outcome of dyadic contests. We hypothesized that competitors would adjust their strategies based on the context of the competition, and thus, we aimed to identify the factors that contributed to such decision-making. Our findings showed residency as the primary driver of competitive strategy, wherein residents had higher aggression and feeding when compared to intruders. The developmental stage had a significant effect on feeding, increasing from young to older stages, but body size contrasts did not contribute significantly towards the outcome of the contests. For the species effect, T emerged as a winner in most of the interspecific contests, exhibiting a significant amount of total aggression. However, GC showed distinct behavioural strategies when competing against T versus conspecifics, and exhibited higher levels of aggression and reduced hiding during intra- when compared to interspecific trials. Surprisingly, the feeding behaviour of GC was not significantly impacted in the presence of T, possibly because GC used hiding as a defence strategy, emphasizing the context-dependent, strategic thinking of the species. Overall, the variety of behavioural tactics exhibited by GC in staged competitive interactions showcases robust survival skills of the species, a key trait that may help maintain its fitness in challenging ecological habitats.

papers.title: AT1R-Selective Negative Allosteric Modulator Targeting the Epitope for Pathogenic Autoantibody Activation
papers.abstract: A major therapeutic strategy for managing cardiovascular and renal diseases is the use of angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). These drugs block both pathogenic and physiological signaling by the angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) by preventing angiotensin II (AngII) binding to orthosteric pocket in transmembrane portion of AT1R. However, in many autoimmune diseases, AT1R activation is chronically driven by pathogenic autoantibody binding to a distinct extracellular surface located allosteric site. Currently, there are no allosteric inhibitors of AT1R available to mechanistically prevent the autoantibodies and preserve the orthosteric hormonal functions of AngII. Here, we report the structure-guided hit-to-lead optimization of TP1, a first-in-class AT1R allosteric chemotype and negative allosteric modulator (NAM) with improved potency and drug-like properties. Computational docking and site-directed mutagenesis identified a TP1 binding mode that is distinct from the orthosteric-site binding of ARBs and AngII. Synthetically pure TP1 significantly reduced the capacity of AT1R to bind AngII without affecting AngII binding to AT2R, demonstrating an AT1R selective effect. TP1 reduced AngII-induced calcium signaling and migration in AT1R-expressing cells, arterial contraction, and increases in blood pressure in AngII-infused mice, demonstrating its activity as a NAM. Crucially, TP1 blocked binding of pathogenic autoantibodies to AT1R-expressing cells from the serum of patients with preeclampsia and dilated cardiomyopathy, a function distinct from ARBs. Together, these findings establish TP1 as a proof-of-concept, AT1R-selective NAM chemotype with therapeutic potential for AT1R autoantibody-driven conditions such as preeclampsia, where ARBs are strictly contraindicated. Developing AT1R-targeted NAM antihypertensive drugs may offer therapeutic advantages over ARBs and expand the pharmacological toolkit for this important CVD receptor. Key words: AT1R, AngII, AT1R-AAb, NAM, Allosteric ligand, GPCR, blood pressure, pharmacokinetics, antihypertensives

papers.title: Birth synchronisation increases allonursing opportunities in free-ranging dogs
papers.abstract: Over 50 years ago, the hypothesis emerged that co-resident women synchronise menstruation through pheromonal cues. This idea has persisted as a widespread narrative and has subsequently been extrapolated to other animals as well. Indeed, reproductive synchrony has many potential benefits, including creating allonursing opportunities and facilitating female mate choice. Nevertheless, little evidence exists of female vertebrates synchronising their oestrus beyond seasonal effects, through socially mediated cues. We analysed reproductive synchrony in free-ranging dogs, which combine weak, population-dependent reproductive seasonality with facultative cooperative breeding. Controlling for seasonality, we show that birth synchrony was higher among co-resident, maternally related females, suggesting synchronisation among individuals who are likely to cooperate. This was supported by our finding that birth synchrony and maternal kinship independently increased the probability and frequency of allonursing. Finally, preliminary evidence shows that oestrus synchrony decreased male monopolisation. These findings contribute to the debate on socially mediated reproductive synchronisation, suggesting that it may have mainly evolved because it facilitates cooperative breeding.

papers.title: Development of a nanomedicine approach to improve the therapeutic index of bexarotene.
papers.abstract: Bexarotene (BEX), a retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist, has demonstrated therapeutic potential in oncology, neurodegenerative diseases and inflammatory conditions, including multiple sclerosis (MS). However, its broader clinical application is limited by poor aqueous solubility, low bioavailability, and dose-limiting adverse effects, most notably hypertriglyceridaemia. In this study, we investigated whether conjugation of BEX to dextrin, a biodegradable polysaccharide, could improve its physicochemical properties and therapeutic index. A dextrin-BEX conjugate was synthesised using succinoylated dextrin (30 mol%) and characterised by gel permeation chromatography (GPC), Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). The effects of conjugation on solubility, aggregation behaviour and biological activity were evaluated using in vitro cytotoxicity assays in leukaemia, liver and fibroblast cell lines, alongside measurements of intracellular triglyceride levels. The impact on lipid metabolism and toxicity was further assessed in an in vivo murine model of hyperlipidaemia. Dextrin conjugation significantly increased the aqueous solubility of BEX (from <0.004 mg/mL to 9.88 mg/mL) and led to the formation of nanoscale aggregates in solution. This was associated with a marked increase in in vitro potency, with IC50 values reduced by up to 14-fold across multiple cell lines. However, the increased cytotoxicity was not selective for cancer cells and was also observed in normal fibroblast and hepatic cell models. The dextrin-BEX conjugate did not induce intracellular triglyceride accumulation in vitro. In vivo, dextrin conjugation did not mitigate BEX-associated lipid dysregulation, while serum triglyceride levels and markers of liver injury remained unchanged. However, although free BEX led to a significant increase in liver weight after 14 days, the dextrin-BEX conjugate did not produce a statistically significant effect. In conclusion, dextrin conjugation markedly improves the solubility and in vitro potency of BEX but does not enhance its selectivity or reduce its metabolic toxicity in vivo. These findings suggest that while polymer conjugation is an effective strategy for addressing physicochemical limitations, it is insufficient to overcome the inherent dyslipidaemia associated with systemic RXR activation. Future strategies should focus on integrating targeting and controlled release mechanisms, alongside approaches that address the underlying pharmacological drivers of lipid dysregulation.

papers.title: Social Decision-Making in Response to Competing Stimuli
papers.abstract: Animals routinely encounter diverse social stimuli that can be simultaneous and vary in salience, valence and relevance in regard to ongoing behavioral decisions. Understanding how animals weigh such competing information is crucial for revealing the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying context-dependent social behavior. Here, we investigated how male Astatotilapia burtoni navigate situations in which they must choose between rival males, potential mates, or both socially relevant cues. We first quantified focal male engagement toward stimulus types and found that males prioritized stimuli based on identity, context, and inferred threat level. We then examined the underlying neural correlates of these decisions in the preoptic area (POA) and area Dm (the putative teleost homolog of the basolateral amygdala (area Dm), two key nodes of the social decision-making network (SDMN). Using phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6 (pS6) as a marker of neural activity and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) to identify dopaminergic cell populations, we found that overall activity of these brain regions as well as the activity of dopaminergic cell populations did not differ between the different social stimulus treatments. Our results reveal how animals navigate complex environments involving multiple social cues and highlight the behavioral and neural mechanisms supporting stimulus prioritization.

papers.title: Arsenic Impairs Critical Cellular Events of Human Cardiac Development Across Differentiation and Metabolic Maturation
papers.abstract: Arsenic (As) is a widespread environmental contaminant, with exposure occurring primarily through contaminated food and water or cigarette smoke. Maternal exposure to As represents a significant risk factor for congenital heart disease in offspring. However, the mechanisms underlying As induced developmental cardiotoxicity remain poorly defined. Pluripotent stem cells provide an excellent platform for studying mechanisms of developmental toxicity. Embryoid bodies (EBs) derived from stem cells, can recapitulate many key events of early embryogenesis including germ layers specification. Human cardiomyocytes are derived from mesodermal progenitors. NKX2.5 governs cardiac specification and morphogenesis, and its mutation produces atrial and ventricular defects in humans. Using an NKX2.5 reporter stem cell line, we modeled mesoderm differentiation in EBs and cardiac induction in a 2D cardiomyocyte differentiation system. In an 8 day differentiation protocol, As (0.05 M; 3.75 ppb) significantly suppressed cardiomyocyte differentiation and cardiac induction. However, As increased mesodermal markers (HAND1, SNAI2, HOPX) gene expression. In contrast, cardiac specific genes, including NKX2.5, GATA4, Troponin T, and alpha actinin, were markedly downregulated in the presence of As. As also reduced expression of genes related to cardiac induction, fibroblast function, and vascular markers in the cardiac organoid model. As impaired cardiomyocyte maturation related gene expressions at concentrations without affecting cardiomyocyte proliferation. In a zebrafish model of early heart development, As increased heart rate and disrupted ion channel gene expression. In conclusion, As inhibits ESC differentiation into cardiomyocytes and disrupts cardiomyocyte maturation. Combining stem cell derived models with zebrafish exposure, this study illuminates adverse outcome pathways for As induced congenital heart defect.

papers.title: Neprilysin 1 in the Mushroom Body controls Feeding behavior by regulating SIFamide levels in Drosophila melanogaster
papers.abstract: Feeding-related behavior in Drosophila melanogaster encompasses olfactory and gustatory detection of odors, foraging, and food intake. In Drosophila melanogaster, the neuropeptide SIFamide (SIFa), has been shown to integrate hunger signals to promote feeding in Drosophila and is considered a central regulator of mutually exclusive behavioral states. Here, we identify the mushroom bodies as a key downstream circuit of SIFamidergic neurons for regulation of food-seeking and feeding. Furthermore, we show that mushroom bodies are not merely downstream effectors but actively shape SIFamidergic signaling through the peptidase Neprilysin 1 for which SIFamide is a substrate. Thus, SIFa signaling is embedded within a feedforward-feedback circuit that couples internal state to the selection and execution of feeding behavior. We propose that the distinct neuronal subtypes postsynaptic to the elaborately arborized SIFamidergic neurons define discrete neuronal subroutines that differentially control the mutually exclusive behaviors related to sexual reproduction, sleep and feeding. Our findings reveal an evolutionary ancient peptidergic system that is modified by recruitment of novel genes for the flexible control of distinct behavioral programs and feeding strategies.

papers.title: The social structure of a captive group of Rüppell's vultures (Gyps rueppellii)
papers.abstract: Studies on the evolution of intelligence have so far mainly focused on mammals, primates in particular, and only few avian taxa, mainly corvids and parrots. Vultures, however, have relatively large brains too, and those of the Gyps genus are highly social. Their obligate scavenging lifestyle and sociality make them an excellent taxon for investigating the role of social and ecological selective pressures on the evolution of intelligence. However, little is known of Gyps vultures, particularly regarding their social complexity (sensu Social Brain Hypothesis). To investigate the complexity within their social structure, we studied the dominance hierarchy and social bonds of a captive group (n {equiv} 23) of Ruppell's vultures (Gyps rueppellii) over two consecutive years. Our results revealed that dominance ranks and affiliative bonds were stable, although there were some differences between breeding and non-breeding seasons. During the breeding season, pair-bonded individuals were more dominant and less social than unpaired individuals. Pair-bond status, age and season influenced dyadic bond strength. Most notably, pair-bonded dyads had substantially stronger bonds, but maintained multiple other strong bonds, too. Our results highlight that multiple forces shape the dominance hierarchy and affiliative network of captive Ruppell's vultures. Individual characteristics shape social bonds, social relationships are differentiated, and changes between the breeding and non-breeding season can result in social uncertainty, adding to the complexity of this system. The complexity of Ruppell's vultures' social structure seems comparable to that of some social corvid and parrot species, where it has been linked to their sophisticated cognition. Future socio-cognitive work on this and other less social vulture species could further identify the social challenges they face, and reveal whether a complex social environment may have been a selection pressure on the evolution of intelligence, both in general, and in this promising new taxonomic group for cognition studies specifically.

papers.title: Active teaching-learning methodology in a non-formal teaching environment as a tool to mitigate the "plant awareness disparity" in public school students.
papers.abstract: Currently, a significant proportion of young people are discouraged by the teaching of botany and, consequently, show little interest in preserving local biodiversity. On the other hand, with the recurrent use of digital technologies (DTs), young people have shown significant interest in virtual devices. Our project's tested the hypothesis whether plants awareness disparity in public school students was overcome through active teaching and learning. Thus, the objective was to investigate the use of active methodology in a non-formal teaching environment (e.g., sensory garden, SG) in order to stimulate learning in plant organography based on its evaluation using digital games. Our proposal was investigated at the Lagoa do Sino campus (Buri/SP, Brazil) in partnership with the Public School System of the Municipality of Campina do Monte Alegre/SP, Brazil. Furthermore, students were divided into two teams, which applied qualitative methodologies, such as that one of these (Team A) had face-to-face contact with the SG, using the Problem-Based Learning (PBL) methodology, digital game and survey. Team B, on the other hand, will only have contact with the game. After collecting the data, we verified statistically significant differences between the teams using the Wilcoxon test and based on the latent traits evaluated. Given this, the literature points out that discouraging students influences their learning and, consequently, their education. In addition, our considerations are based on the latent trait knowledge of botany and, thus, we reject our null hypothesis and accept our alternative hypothesis. On the other hand, based on the latent trait of plant perception, we cannot affirm the acceptance or rejection of the hypotheses. It is worth noting that future studies should have a larger number of participants than this research in order to better evaluate what is intended.

papers.title: Phosphorylation of β-arrestins impacts recruitment to Parathyroid Hormone Receptor 1 (PTH1R) at the cell surface and endosomes
papers.abstract: {beta}-arrestins 1 and 2 are intracellular adaptor proteins that regulate the subcellular localisation and signalling of GPCRs including Parathyroid Hormone Receptor 1 (PTH1R), which produces {beta}-arrestin-dependent signalling that may selectively stimulate bone anabolism. {beta}-arrestins can themselves be regulated by post-translational modifications including phosphorylation, which dictates the translocation and signalling of the few GPCRs studied in this context to date. We aimed to investigate whether phosphorylation of {beta}-arrestins modulates their subcellular translocation in response to PTH1R activation. Translocation of {beta}-arrestins to the plasma membrane and early endosomes was quantified using BRET biosensors and immunocytochemistry with high content analysis. Phosphoknockout or phosphomimetic mutations were introduced to previously demonstrated phosphorylation sites in {beta}-arrestins 1 and 2, initially in bulk to assess overall effects. Plasma membrane translocation was altered only subtly, whereas early endosome translocation was markedly reduced for both mutations but to a greater degree for the phosphomimetic. Contributions of individual or paired sites were assessed by restoration to wildtype from the bulk phosphomimetic mutants. Dual restoration of S13 and T275 in {beta}-arrestin 1, or the analogous sites in {beta}-arrestin 2, restored the greatest degrees of early endosomal translocation, with complete restoration for {beta}-arrestin 1 and partial for {beta}-arrestin 2. Restoration of other sites had minimal or no effect. Dephosphorylation therefore appears to be required for PTH1R-stimulated {beta}-arrestin early endosomal translocation, with different phosphorylation sites implicated than some other GPCRs. These findings raise the possibility of differential {beta}-arrestin regulation by distinct stimuli which may have implications in therapeutic targeting of {beta}-arrestin-dependent pathways.

papers.title: Cell Painting and machine learning for mechanistic profiling of hepatotoxic botanicals and their constituents
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.

papers.title: Individual behavioral signatures shape processing of context-dependent social fear
papers.abstract: Context processing is an essential function in the cognitive repertoire of numerous species, including humans and mice, allowing them to learn from their environment and adapt their future behavior. Impairments or alterations in context processing are hypothesized to represent one of the core etiological mechanisms underlying trauma- and stressor-related disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Individual behavioral traits are key determinants of post-stress responses; however, how they influence distinct phases of contextual encoding and processing remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap is further exacerbated by the limited availability of contextual fear protocols based on social stress, even though the latter is among the most frequent and impactful forms of stress exposure. Here, based on social defeat paradigms, we establish a longitudinal social conditioned place aversion (sCPA) protocol that leads to avoidance of the defeat-associated chamber in adult male mice. Prior characterization of mice according to anxiety-related phenotypes revealed that mice displaying high novelty-induced thigmotaxic (i.e. high anxiety-like) behavior showed lasting long-term memory of the defeat-associated chamber as denoted by persistent avoidance. On the other hand, lower levels of exploration/locomotor behaviors prior to stress exposure predicted greater avoidance of the defeat-associated chamber in the short-term. Finally, we reveal that inhibiting the activity of VTAVgat neurons during conditioning sessions abolished sCPA acquisition, while disrupting the predictive ability of locomotor/exploratory profiles derived prior to the sCPA. Our data establishes a robust temporally structured social stress-based conditioning protocol and reveals how prior individual anxiety- and exploration/locomotion-related traits influence distinct stages of context processing.

papers.title: Rate dependent Effects of AMPH on attentional processes as measured by 5C-CPT task
papers.abstract: Background: ADHD is characterized by inattention and impulsivity. Stimulants such as amphetamine are the first line treatments for ADHD. Amphetamine (AMPH) works by increasing extracellular levels of dopamine and noradrenaline. Such stimulants are used to test predictive validity of animal tasks, where it has been reported that amphetamine improves rat 5-CSRTT accuracy when the session length is increased to 250 trials. This improvement in accuracy was observed later in the session as control performance declined. Proving that amphetamine can improve 5C-CPT task performance adds to the predictive validity of the task. No previous works has demonstrated the pro-attentional effects of amphetamine on sustained attention in rat 5C-CPT. We have previously shown that pharmacological manipulations of dopaminergic system improve waiting impulsivity in a rate dependent manner and the importance of analysing the data using Oldham method. The present study extends this work to investigate the effect of amphetamine on attentional processes. Objective: to investigate effects of amphetamine on attentional processes as measured by 5C-CPT task using correlational analysis and group performance. Methods: Trained female Lister hooded rats were tested with AMPH (0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 mg/kg) under reduced stimulus duration schedule (0.25,0.5,1,1.5 and 2s SD) over normal length session (120 trials). Correlational analysis (Oldham method) was used to understand the relationship between baseline performance measures and the change following administration of AMPH. Results: The highest dose of AMPH impaired attentional performance in the 5C-CPT under reduced SD challenge (0.5s,1s,1.5s and 2s). This impairment was due to increase in FAR. Previous studies in 5-CSRTT suggest that reducing the SD increases attentional demand in the form of reducing accuracy without affecting waiting impulsivity. However, the 5-CSRTT does not include non-target trials, therefore, it cannot be used to measure sustained attention (SI) and responsivity index. The 5C-CPT requires greater attentional resources than the 5-CSRTT.This study is the first to report that reducing the SD changes responsivity index (bias) rather than measures of sustained attention (sensitivity index) in the 5C-CPT. Control sensitivity index did not change until the SD was reduced to less than 0.5s and this change was due to a change in baseline responsivity index (bias). Performance under each reduced SD revealed that the highest dose of AMPH (0.4 mg/kg) showed a tendency toward reducing sensitivity index at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5s SDs. Under 1.0s SD, the highest dose of AMPH changed sustained attention (SI, HR and FAR) and omission in a rate-dependent manner without changing responsivity index. Performance across the session revealed that the impairment in sustained attention was observed at the beginning of the session. In the third trial block, Oldham method revealed an inverse relationship between baseline accuracy and the change following administration of 0.2 mg/kg AMPH, indicative of a rate-dependent effect. Conclusions: This study successfully demonstrates rate-dependent effects of AMPH on measures of attentional performance in the 5C-CPT. This experiment also demonstrates that responsivity index is sensitive to reduced SD challenge. To our knowledge this is the first study to report the presence of a direct relationship between baseline sustained attention and magnitude of improvement following administration of 0.4 mg/kg AMPH and an inverse relationship between baseline accuracy and the change following administration of 0.2 mg/kg AMPH in 5C-CPT task. Future studies should test lower doses of amphetamine (0.05 and 0.1 mg/kg) over extended session length (250 trials) to reveal the pro-attentional effects of this drug on 5C-CPT performance measures.

papers.title: EthoTrace: from behaviour to neural dynamics in a unified analysis framework
papers.abstract: Understanding how neural populations support natural behaviour requires knowing what a population does while an animal performs a specific, self-initiated action. For responses evoked by an experimenter-delivered stimulus, the signal can be aligned by the trigger itself, and no behavioural scoring is needed to define the event. Complex behaviours such as parental care and social interaction provide no such trigger. They are defined from the video record, usually offline and post hoc, and are conventionally scored in one program and exported to another for analysis. In this study we developed EthoTrace, a single self-contained HTML file that runs in a desktop browser without installation, server or network access and carries a session from behaviour and calcium signal through to the statistical comparison. Behaviour is annotated on a timeline shared with the {Delta}F/F trace, the signal is corrected and scaled under a stated baseline convention, single bouts stay inspectable in their behavioural context, and repeated bouts are aligned without filling absent data. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a parenting behaviour experiment, in which behaviour was scored and the photometry signal analysed in a single session folder. We expect EthoTrace to facilitate integrative analysis in neuroscience, where behavioural observation and fiber photometry signals are interpreted together.

papers.title: Sex-Specific Development in the Persistence of Stress-Induced Enhancement of Fear Learning in Juvenile and Adult Rats
papers.abstract: It is estimated that approximately fifty percent of the population will encounter at least one traumatic event during their lifetime; however, only six percent develop Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), a trauma-related disorder characterized by persistent alterations in affect and cognition, including an exaggerated fear response. It is well established that females (9.7%) are more than twice as likely as males (3.6%) to be diagnosed with PTSD. Nevertheless, a significant challenge remains in understanding how the severity of traumas experienced in childhood versus adulthood influences PTSD development across sexes. To address this challenge effectively, the adoption of preclinical animal models that accurately reflect these key characteristics is crucial. The Stress Enhanced Fear Learning (SEFL) paradigm in rodents encapsulates some of these complexities associated with PTSD, such as persistent fear sensitization following exposure to acute trauma. This study investigates how stress severity and developmental timing affect the long-term maintenance of SEFL in male and female rats. Juvenile and adult rats were initially subjected to no stress (control, context only), low stress (1 footshock), moderate stress (3 footshocks), or high stress (15 footshocks), followed by an extinction session either one day (recent) or sixty days (remote) later. Subsequently, to evaluate SEFL in a new context, all subjects received a single footshock and were tested the following day. Shortly after stress induction, all groups displayed SEFL. Although the effects persisted for sixty days in adult males and juvenile females, even at the lowest stress level, they were significantly reduced in juvenile males and adult females. These findings offer novel insights into sex-related differences in the persistence of SEFL and introduce new considerations regarding how the timing of developmental stressors influences future threat encoding and fear responses.
